flow.title: Flow
flow.body:
Each of Flow's own screens has a page of help like this one: press **F1** while it's open (the command history, Settings and its color picker, the assistant's panel, the key dialog), or **{help}** anywhere. A link opens its page: click it, or choose it with Tab and press Enter. Esc goes back to the page before, and on the first page closes help, as the same key does at once. In the terminal, F1 is the program's: many use it for help of their own.

# Keys
- Every key here can be changed: [Flow's keys](help:keys) lists them all as they're bound, and Settings' **Keys** changes them.
- {split_right} splits the pane in front in two side by side, and {split_down} one above the other; {pane_move} and the arrows move between panes, a click gives one the keys, and {close_tab} closes the pane in front first, as does the ✕ at the top right of the pane under the pointer (or a theme's frame's close box). Each pane wears a theme of its own, which Settings on it changes.
- {new_tab} opens a tab with the default shell (the **+** in the title bar [lists every shell](help:shells)), {close_tab} closes it (where something runs in it, a toast says what, and closing it again ends it), and {pick_tab} shows tab 1 to 9. A tab without a name of its own is called after its shell and keeps its number (**zsh 2**) as others close. Double-click a tab to give it a name of your own, or choose **Rename Tab** in the [command palette](help:palette): Enter keeps it, Esc puts back the one before, and a name left empty gives the tab its shell's name again. Flow keeps the names with the tabs it opens again. **New Group** in the palette puts the tab in front into a group of its own, a bar in its color under each of its tabs; **Move Tab to Group** moves it into another, **Remove Tab from Group** takes it out, and **Go to Tab** finds any tab by its name. A tab you open from one in a group joins it, and Flow keeps the groups with the tabs. A right click on a tab opens its menu: Rename, Move to New Group or another group, Remove from Group, Restart Tab and Close.
- [The tab sidebar](help:tabs)
- {copy} copies what's selected, and {paste} pastes.
- {bigger}, {smaller} and {reset} change the font's size.
- {history} searches the [command history](help:history).
- {find} [finds words in the scrollback](help:find).
- Scrolled back, a pill at the terminal's top right says how many lines are below: click it, or press {scroll_bottom}, to go back down; {scroll_top} goes to the top. {previous_command} and {next_command} go from one command run to the next, each marked on the scrollbar where its prompt was (a failed one in red). The scrollbar along the right edge goes anywhere in between: drag it, or click where to go. Settings' **Scrollbar** (under Terminal) shows it while scrolling, always or never.
- {assistant} opens the [assistant's panel](help:assistant), and closes it.
- {settings} opens [Settings](help:settings).
- {palette} opens the [command palette](help:palette): every command, setting, theme and page, found by typing.
- {efficient} turns efficient mode on and off, as **🌱e-mode** in the title bar does: the liquid, the CRT, effects and the theme's sounds pause for real work.
- **on-top** in the title bar keeps Flow's window in front of every other window, and turns that off again (Settings' **Always on top**; on the Mac, **Window → Float on Top**). [Settings](help:settings)' Keys can give it a key.
- {record} records the terminal to an animated WebP, the liquid and the tube in it, while a clock in the title bar runs; {record} again, or a click on the clock, stops it, and the system's save panel asks where to keep it.
- {restart} restarts the tab in front: its shell ends and starts again in its place, greeting you with the startup logo as Flow does when it starts, and the other tabs stay as they are. While a program runs in it, it asks first: press {restart} again to end it and restart. Settings' **Restart** restarts all of Flow.
- A click on the Flow logo shows [About Flow](help:about).

# The mouse
Over a program that takes the mouse (an editor, a game, `htop`), hold Shift to select, open the menu or scroll back.

At the shell's prompt, a click on the line you're typing moves the cursor there, as the arrow keys would; anywhere else a click selects. Settings' **Click to move the cursor** turns it off.

A link a program writes (OSC 8, such as an app's name in `flowapp list`) is underlined under the pointer, and where it goes shows at the terminal's foot: hold {jump} and click to open it. Flow opens web and mail links, and shows a link to a file on this computer in its folder, never running it.

# Pages
In a tab, `flow-help` prints every page, and `flow-help settings` one of them.
- [Flow's keys](help:keys)
- [Command history](help:history)
- [Find in the scrollback](help:find)
- [The command palette](help:palette)
- [The assistant](help:assistant)
- [Settings](help:settings)
- [Picking a color](help:picker)
- [The theme gallery](help:gallery)
- [The API key](help:key)
- [A 3D model from a file](help:model)
- [A new tab](help:shells)
- [Flow's apps](help:apps)
- [The flow command](help:command)
- [Outside apps](help:outside)
- [A server asks](help:server_ask)
- [About Flow](help:about)
- [Checking for updates](help:updates)
- [Legal](help:legal)

keys.title: Flow's keys
keys.intro: Every key Flow takes, as it's bound now. Settings' **Keys** changes any of them: press Enter on one (or click Change), then the key it's to be; Esc keeps it as it was, and Backspace leaves it none. **Add Key** gives a command another key beside those it has. Only the keys you change are kept, under `[keys]` in config.toml. A key the shell would otherwise get, such as Ctrl and a letter, is said so as Flow takes it. More in [Settings](help:settings).
keys.fixed:
These stay as they are.
- **F1** opens help for the screen in front; over the terminal it's the program's.
- **Esc** closes what's open, **Enter** does what it offers first, and Tab and the arrows move through it.
- {find_pattern} in the find bar searches by a pattern.
- {new_conversation} in the assistant's panel starts a new conversation, and Tab there changes its mode.
- {forget} in the command history forgets the command chosen, and {forget_all} every one found.
- {word} and {word_delete} move and delete by word where you type, and {jump} with the arrows by line.
- Shift+Page Up and Shift+Page Down scroll back a page, as Page Up and Page Down do alone on the Mac outside a full-screen program.
- Off the Mac, Ctrl+C copies while something's selected (otherwise it's the shell's), Ctrl+Insert copies, and Ctrl+V and Shift+Insert paste.
- {jump} and a click opens a link.
- {quit} quits Flow, as every app does.

history.title: Command history
history.body:
{history} opens the command history over the tab in front (on the Mac, **Edit → Search Command History…** does too, as does the menu a right click opens), and Esc closes it.

# Finding a command
Type any words in a command, in any order and any case: every command holding them all shows, the most recently run first, each once with how often it ran. Any three letters in a row find one too, in any script, so `uil` finds `cargo build`.

# Filters
Tab steps through them: **All**, **This folder** (the folder the tab is in), **Failed** (commands that ended in an error) and the tab's shell.

# Using one
↑↓ choose, and Enter or a click puts the command at the prompt, in place of what's typed there, to run or change first. Nothing runs until you press Enter at the prompt. A control character in it (Esc, Ctrl+C, Ctrl+O and the like), which the shell or the terminal would take as a key, is left out; a line break stays, and so does a tab where the shell takes a paste whole (zsh, a newer bash), but not where it doesn't (macOS's own bash, BusyBox's ash, cmd), which takes a tab as a key too. A command holding letters past ASCII isn't put at all where the shell may take them as keys, not letters (bash just after its locale changed into one that isn't UTF-8, or a shell where Flow's hook doesn't run): a note says so.

# Forgetting
{forget} forgets the command chosen. {forget_all}, pressed twice, forgets every command the search finds, so the folder filter with no words forgets a folder's commands.

# What's kept
Each command run in Flow's tabs, whatever the shell, with its folder, how it ended and when. Commands [the assistant](help:assistant) ran wear its ✦; it looks in the history only when you ask after a command you ran before. Never kept: a line that starts with a space, or one that looks like it sets a secret (a password, a token or a key).

[Settings](help:settings)' **Command history** turns it off, and **Kept commands** says how many there are, with **Clear**, pressed twice, to forget them all.

find.title: Find in the scrollback
find.body:
{find} opens the find bar at the terminal's top right (on the Mac, **Edit → Find…** does too). It searches the tab's text: its screen and everything scrolled off it. Esc closes it.

# Finding
Type what to look for. It's found as written, letters and signs alike, and in any case unless you type a capital letter. Every match is lit, the one chosen brighter, and the bar says which of how many it is. If you've selected a few words in the terminal when you open it, they're looked for at once.

# Patterns
The bar's `.*`, or {find_pattern}, looks for what you type as a pattern, a regular expression: `build \d+` finds every build and its number, `took|failed` either word. It's lit while it's on, and "Bad pattern" takes the count's place while what's typed isn't one. A capital letter still asks for its case. Click it, or press {find_pattern} again, to look for text as written.

# Moving between matches
↑ or Enter goes to the match before, further up the scrollback, and ↓ or Shift+Enter to the one after; {find_next} and {find_previous} do too. Past the first or the last it goes round. The terminal scrolls to show each one. The matches are marked down the pane's scrollbar too, the one chosen taller, and a click on a mark scrolls there.

# While it's open
The matches follow what's printed. A click in the terminal gives the terminal the keys back, and the bar stays showing its matches; a click on the bar, or {find} again, gives them back to the bar. In another tab it searches that tab for the same.

palette.title: The command palette
palette.body:
{palette} opens the command palette over everything (on the Mac, **View → Command Palette…** does too), and Esc closes it.

# Finding
Type a few letters of what you want, in order and in any case: `nt` finds **New Tab**, `opa` the glass's **Opacity**, and a setting is found by its section too, so `glass opa` finds it as well. A setting is found by any words about it as well, as Settings' search finds it: what its hint says, its choices (`amber` finds **Phosphor**) and its key in config.toml (`fx.crt`), after what's found by name. A letter that starts a word, or follows the last one found, counts most, so the best match comes first. What you chose lately comes first before anything's typed, and ahead of others that match as well.

# What's in it
- **Commands:** everything in Flow's menus, with its keys: tabs, copy and paste, find, the history, text size, efficient mode, recording the terminal, the assistant and its key, Settings, help, About, restart and quit.
- **Settings:** every row, which opens [Settings](help:settings) at it.
- **Themes:** every theme, which the tab in front puts on, as Settings' Theme row does.
- **Help:** every page of help.
- **New tab:** a tab in each shell, as the [new-tab picker](help:shells) opens one.
- **Tabs:** **Go to Tab** for each tab, by its name, and for the tab in front **Move Tab to Group** for each group and **Remove Tab from Group**. These aren't kept among what you chose lately.

# Choosing
↑ and ↓ choose, Page Up and Page Down by eight, and the wheel scrolls. Enter, or a click, does what's chosen and closes the palette.

assistant.title: The assistant
assistant.body:
Say what you want in your own words, and Enter sends it. The assistant can run commands in the tab in front, read the screen, and read and write files; it sees your system, the shell, its folder and the screen's last lines.

# Typing
The input grows a row at a time as what you type wraps, up to a third of the panel, and Shift+Enter starts a new line; a paste keeps its lines. A click puts the caret there, a drag or Shift+click selects, a double click takes a word and a triple click its line. Shift with the arrows selects too, {word} with them goes by words, {input_rows} go to a row's ends and {input_ends} to the text's. {input_select_all} selects it all, {input_copy} copies, {input_cut} cuts and {dialog_paste} pastes, over what's selected; {input_undo} undoes and {input_redo} does it again. Esc lets go of a selection first.

↑ on the first row brings back the message (or `/` command) you sent before, and ↓ on the last goes forward again, then back to what you were typing. A change you make to one is kept while you go through them, until you send. The last 200 come back after Flow restarts too, while Memory is on.

# Guide and auto
Tab switches between them, and the panel's header says which is on.
- **Guide:** every command, file read and file write waits for your yes.
- **Auto:** it runs commands itself, but what it rates high risk still waits, and so does what Flow's own rules flag: deleting, `sudo`, restarting, piping a download into a shell or sending data to another machine, force-pushes, a command that reads or names a file that looks like a secret, reading such a file, and overwriting a file.

Flow's rules are a check by pattern, not a sandbox: they read a command as it's written, and many of the ways a program's name is spelled or wrapped read as that program (`/bin/rm`, `\r\m`, `'rm'`, `env rm`, `sh -c "rm …"`); they ask about any whose program they can't read for certain (a variable, `$(…)`, a glob such as `/bin/r?`, what `xargs` or `eval` runs), a shell handed its program from elsewhere (`… | sh`), and a line the shell would change before it runs (a control character in it, `!!`). So a command built from a variable asks, however harmless; written out, it runs as any other. A command can still do what its words don't say (a script, `python -c`, a path built as it runs), so in auto mode, and while it works on its own, the assistant can run commands the rules don't recognize as risky. Guide mode asks before every one.

In either mode, a file on another computer (`\\server\share\…`; on Windows, any path but a drive's) is never read or written for it: it's refused without asking, as a link or a folder a program printed could lead the assistant there, and on Windows merely opening it hands that computer your sign-in. On Windows a command naming such a path waits for your yes, in auto mode too.

# A command waiting
Enter runs it, **E** edits it first, and **S** skips it. Type something and press Enter to decline it and say why.

# Files
Drop a file on the panel to give it to the assistant with your next message: a picture (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP), a PDF, a text file, or a Word, Excel or PowerPoint file. **Attach** at the input's end picks files the same way, and pasting a picture (a screenshot) into the panel adds it too. Each waits as a chip over the input, ✕ taking it off, until you press Enter, with words or without. A large picture is made smaller first. A file dropped on the terminal types its path there instead, quoted for the shell.

A file that looks like a secret (a key, a `.env`, what's under `.ssh`) waits on its orange chip until you click it. The assistant's `read_file` reads pictures, PDFs and Office files too, asking as it asks for any file. Only a file's name goes into the assistant's memory, never what's in it.

# Copying and running
Under a block of code in a reply, **Copy** copies it, and for commands **Run** runs them in the tab in front, as if typed there; a command rated high risk, or several lines where the shell can't take them as written, is put at the prompt instead, for you to check and run with Enter. A shell session's output lines don't run. A line that's nothing but something in backticks, such as a file's name or a command, has a small **Copy** at its end, and so has the card of a command the assistant ran or is waiting to run. Over a reply, **Copy reply** copies all of it. A drag over the conversation selects its words, to copy as in the terminal.

# Ask why
When a command you ran fails (anything but Ctrl+C's stop), **✦ Ask why** shows at the terminal's foot once the shell's prompt is back. Click it, or choose **Ask Why It Failed** (the Assistant menu on the Mac, or the [command palette](help:palette)), and the panel opens and asks why it failed and how to fix it, with the end of what it printed. The assistant suggests; it runs nothing unless you say. It goes once the next command starts. cmd says nothing of how a command ended, so it never shows there.

# Where it works
The assistant types its commands into your pane while it's free. While your shell is busy, or you've typed something at its prompt, it opens a pane of its own beside yours, labelled **Assistant**, and works there; [Settings](help:settings)' **Where it works** can have it always use its own. A new conversation closes that pane. Which pane a command goes to is settled as Flow judges it, in the folder that pane's shell is in, and it goes there: one you say yes to runs where it was going when its card showed, and never over what you've started or typed in your pane since.

# When a command asks something
A command of the assistant's that stops at a question (a password, `[Y/n]`, "Press any key") waits for you rather than timing out: its tab comes to the front, the panel says what's asked, and a notification does while Flow is behind other windows. Answer it in the terminal, not in the panel. The assistant reads what the terminal shows: a password's prompt usually shows nothing of what you type, but whatever the program does show of your answer is in the output it reads.

# Waiting, undo and Flow itself
- For a long build or a service coming up, the assistant can wait without spending tokens: Flow watches for the command to finish, for some text in its output or a file, and tells it then.
- A file the assistant writes is kept as it was first: **Undo** on its card puts it back (or takes away a file it made), `/undo` puts back everything the task changed, and you can ask it to undo its changes.
- It reads Flow's own help, and changes Flow's settings through what `flow-settings` may change: ask it to make the text bigger, or to wear another theme.
- A long conversation has its older turns summed up as it fills, so it goes on; the panel says when.

# The task's steps
For a task of several steps, the assistant shows them in a strip at the top of the panel as it goes: ✓ done, ◌ under way, ○ still to come. Working on its own starts the strip from its plan, and the memory keeps it with the task, so a task carried on after a restart shows where it was.

# Your instructions and skills
Settings' **Your instructions** opens a text file of your own, sent with every conversation: your standing rules and tastes for the assistant ("always use winget", "keep answers short"), followed where they don't get round Flow's approvals. **Skills** opens a folder of playbooks, each a Markdown file (or a folder with a `SKILL.md`) beginning with its `name` and `description`, which the assistant reads when a task matches one. Ask it to keep a procedure that worked as a skill, and it writes one there. `/skills` lists them. Settings' **Skills** section, under the assistant's, has a switch for each skill, and one switched off isn't listed for the assistant. Packages `flowapp` installs may bring skills too (`flow-skills`, Flow's own, or an app's for its commands): they're listed there under **Skills from** and the package's name, as `package:name`, each with a switch of its own, off until you turn it on (**All on** and **All off** turn them all).

# Helpers
For several things to look into at once, the assistant can hand parts of a task to helpers: each works in a pane of its own (**Helper 1**, **Helper 2**), its card in the panel saying what it does and how many tokens it has used, and reports back. At most 3 work at once. A helper that only looks runs only what Flow rates low risk; one that may change things never runs what's high risk, or under working on its own, what that doesn't let. Helpers never ask you anything. Guide mode asks before each helper; auto mode asks only for one that may change things. Their panes close when the assistant's turn ends, and Esc stops them. [Settings](help:settings)' **Helpers** and **Helpers' model** set them.

# Working on its own
For a task of several steps, the assistant may ask to work through it on its own: a card shows its plan, what it asks for (administrator rights, a restart), and how long and how many tokens it may take. **Let it work** (Enter) lets it run its commands without asking until the task is done or its time or tokens run out; **Ask each time** (S) keeps asking. Even then it asks before a command needing what it wasn't let do, before a few things Flow always asks about (erasing disks, deleting a whole drive or home folder, turning off the system's protections, changing accounts and passwords, reading credential stores), before a command whose program Flow can't read from it (`$(…)`, `… | sh`), and before reading, writing or naming files that look like secrets. Flow tells these by pattern, not by watching what a command does, so one it doesn't recognize runs without asking. On the Mac and Linux it runs `sudo -v` first, so you type your password once, in the terminal; a command waiting for a password says so in the panel, and with a notification while Flow is behind other windows. On Windows, administrator rights open Flow again as administrator, in a window of its own, where the task carries on. Esc, or a click on **On its own** in the title bar, stops it. [Settings](help:settings)' **Working on its own**, **Its time** and **Its tokens** set it.

# Memory
Flow keeps a journal of each task on this computer: what you asked (the messages you sent come back with ↑ after a restart), each command the assistant ran with its folder, exit code and the end of its output, and the files it read or wrote. The assistant looks there before trying something again, and keeps lasting facts worth remembering (your computer's GPU, how you install software) in a text file of its own. A new conversation starts with those facts and the last tasks. Nothing that looks like a password, a token or a key is kept.

Before it restarts the computer, it saves where the task stands, and Flow starts again by itself after the restart and offers the task at the foot of the panel: **Carry on** takes it up where it was (Enter in an empty input does the same), and **Not now** leaves it. A task left unfinished in the last week is offered too, once the panel opens. [Settings](help:settings)' **Memory** turns it all off, and **Remembered** opens the facts in your text editor or clears everything. `/memory` lists what's remembered.

# MCP servers
The assistant can use apps that have an MCP server (a notes app, an issue tracker, a database), calling their tools as it runs commands. [Settings](help:settings)' **MCP servers** lists them from `mcp-servers.json` beside config.toml, written as Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Cursor write theirs, so a config can be pasted in (**Open file**). **Add server…** asks for a name, then its command (which Flow starts) or its URL (Streamable HTTP), typed in place. A server starts only once you **Connect** it, and each of its tools is off until you turn it on, so neither the file nor connecting ever changes what the assistant may do. **Approval**, for each server: **Ask each time**, **Read-only without asking** (tools it marks read-only run, the rest ask) or **Without asking**; guide mode always asks. A call's card names the server and the tool, with its arguments: **Run** (Enter), **Edit** (E, its arguments as JSON) or **Skip** (S). Esc gives a call up, and the server is told.

A remote server that needs you to sign in says so: its **Sign-in** row's **Sign in** opens its sign-in in your browser, and Flow keeps what it gives in your system's credential store, refreshing it as it runs out (**Sign out** forgets it). Where the server wants Flow registered by hand, **Client ID…** takes the ID you registered; **Token…** keeps a bearer token of your own instead.

**Its resources**, off until you turn it on, lets the assistant list and read what a server offers to be read (files, records, pages), asking as its Approval says. A server's prompts are ready-made requests: type `/<server>:<prompt>` in the panel, with what it needs after it, and its text goes to the assistant as your message. `/mcp` lists the servers, what each offers and its prompts. A server may also ask you something as it works: see [a server asks](help:server_ask).

# Keys
- Esc stops the assistant, clears what's typed, or goes back to the terminal.
- {new_conversation} starts a new conversation.
- {assistant} opens and closes the panel.
- `/model` opens a list of the models over the input, the one in use marked ●: ↑↓ choose, Enter or a click puts the one chosen in use, its number picks it, and Esc closes the list. `/model` with a name or number puts one in use at once (`/model sonnet`, `/model 2`), as Settings' **Model** does. Another provider's starts a new conversation, and the conversation says which model answers from then on. The list also holds the models the provider in use offers that Flow doesn't list yet, asked of it once a day, so a new one can be chosen before Flow's next release, from the list or by its id.
- `/clear`, `/auto`, `/guide`, `/usage`, `/memory`, `/undo`, `/skills`, `/mcp`, `/settings`, `/about`, `/key` and `/forget` do what they say (`/key` opens the [key dialog](help:key)).

The header counts the tokens used; once they reach [Settings](help:settings)' **Token cap**, the assistant stops before its next request.

settings.title: Settings
settings.body:
↑↓ choose a setting and ←→ change it (Shift moves a slider faster), or use the mouse; the wheel scrolls the list. What you change shows at once, and is saved when Settings closes. The line at the foot says what the chosen setting does.

# Searching
The field at the end of the row of tabs finds a setting by any words about it: its name, what the line at the foot says of it, its choices (amber finds Phosphor) or its key in config.toml (fx.crt), in English as well as in the language Flow is in. Press {find}, or click the field, or just type a letter. Every section is searched, closed ones too: the list shows what's found, the best first, each with its section beside it and the words you typed lit. ↑↓ choose, ←→ change the one chosen there and then, and Enter, or a click on its name, goes to it in its place. Esc empties the field, and then closes Settings.

# Tabs
Settings opens on the tab in front. The row under its title names each open tab, then **New tabs**: click one, or use the tab shortcuts ({pick_tab}, and the keys that go to the next tab and the one before), and that tab comes to the front behind Settings. The look's sections (Theme, Theme details, Liquid, Glass, Text and cursor, and CRT) say **this tab** and change that tab alone, which keeps its look across quitting and Restart; on **New tabs** they change the look new tabs open with. The other sections say **all tabs**: they're Flow's, wherever Settings is.

# Sections
The settings come in sections (General, Theme, Theme details, Liquid, Glass, Text and cursor, CRT, Assistant, Skills, Outside apps, MCP servers, Terminal, Apps, Sound and About), and ↑↓ reach their headers too. Enter or a click on a header closes its section, leaving a count of the settings it hides, and opens it again; ← closes it and → opens it. A section stays as you leave it, so the ones you don't change can stay out of the way; Theme details, the CRT, Apps and Sound start closed. **Collapse all** and **Expand all**, beside Settings' ✕, close every section or open them all, so you can open just the one you want.

# Presets
**Preset file** saves the look (the liquid, glass, glow, CRT, colors, cursor and font) to a file, and loads one, which changes only what it sets. The CRT keeps presets of its own: pick one under **Preset**, or save its parts as they are under a name of yours.

# The CRT
**Strength** turns the tube on, and each of its parts has a row: **Scanlines**, **Interlace**, **Phosphor glow**, **Phosphor decay** (its afterglow), **Grille**, **Vignette** and **Curvature**.

# Font size
**Font size** says what the window holds at it, in characters, and each character's size, as {bigger} and {smaller} do when they change it. **Fit window to**, under it, resizes the window to hold 80 × 24, 80 × 25 or 40 × 25 characters at that size, an old machine's theme putting its own screen first. It resizes it just this once: Flow still opens at the size config.toml gives. Where the screen is too small, the window holds what fits; where the window can't be that small, a toast says from what text size it could. **Fit text to** is the other way round: the window stays, and the text takes the largest whole size at which it holds the screen chosen.

# Colors
A color's row opens a [color picker](help:picker), with help of its own (F1).

# Theme
An old machine's colors, fonts, glass and CRT, with its start screen and prompt (the Flow notanAmiga CLI's first asks for its Workbench disk, which any key puts in, its empty drive clicking until then); or your own theme, after them in the list, whose start screen and prompt you type in place:
- Enter or a click starts typing, with the caret where you click. The arrows, Home and End move ({jump} with them goes to the ends), and {word} with ← or → goes by words; {word_delete} deletes one.
- In the start screen, Enter makes a new line. {done}, Tab or a click elsewhere is done, and Esc puts back what was there.
- A line starting with `^` is centered, `{tall}` makes it double height and `{wide}` double width; `{red}`, `{on-blue}` and the like color it in teletext's colors, `{#d5524d}` and `{on-#d5524d}` in any other, and `{plain}` goes back; `{paper-white}` (or any other color) is the page's, which the lines after it start on and a `{clear}` fills the screen with, until `{paper-plain}`. `{disk}` alone on its line is Kickstart 1.3's picture of a hand holding out the Workbench disk. A centered `{logo}` alone on its line puts the startup logo in the middle, four lines tall. `{wait}` alone on its line waits for the tab's first key (which goes to it, not the shell), `{clear}` clears the screen and `{foot}` goes to its last line.
- `{version}`, `{os}`, `{chip}`, `{memory}` and `{shell}` stand for what they say, and `{cwd}` in the prompt for the folder.

**Theme details**, while an old machine's theme is worn, turns each part of it on or off: its start screen, its prompt, its font, its tube, its colors (programs' sixteen among them, chosen to read on its screen), on the workstations its real numbers (this computer's own Ethernet address and serial in place of made-up ones, which stay the same on it), and each of its sounds, such as the PC's fan. **Cursor speed** sets how fast the cursor glides, and each theme sets its own as it's chosen.

**Save as theme…**, under Theme (and in the [new-tab picker](help:shells), and on the Mac in the View menu), keeps what's worn now under a name you type: the colors (programs' sixteen among them), fonts, cursor, glass, liquid and CRT, with a start screen, prompt and sounds where they're set. It comes after the built-in themes and your own, here and in the picker, and is worn as they are. Chosen here, its start screen and prompt are typed here as your own's are, which changes it and leaves your own as it is. A name already taken is saved over, as the box says. **Export…** writes the one chosen as a theme package, a `.tar.gz` file that `flowapp install` puts among the themes on another computer ([Flow's apps](help:apps)), its fonts named but not carried. **Theme gallery**, under it, shows the packages of themes in flowapp's catalog before you install them ([the theme gallery](help:gallery)). **Apps**, further down, lists flowapp's apps with Install, Upgrade and Remove ([Flow's apps](help:apps)). **Delete** removes the one chosen, leaving its colors, fonts and CRT on under your own theme, and a preset file saved while one is worn moves it too.

# Efficient mode
**Efficient mode**, first in General, or **🌱e-mode** in the title bar ({efficient}), pauses the liquid, the CRT, effects and the theme's sounds, holds a turning startup logo still, and moves the cursor and shows start screens at once. Your settings stay as they are and come back when it's off.

**Efficient on battery**, under it, turns efficient mode on while the computer runs on battery or saves power (the Mac's Low Power Mode, Windows' energy saver), and off again when that ends, unless you turned it on yourself. Meanwhile the title bar reads **🌱e-mode · battery** (or **· low power**). Switch efficient mode off then and it stays off until that ends or Flow quits.

# Hotkey
**Hotkey**, in General, takes a key for the whole system (one of **{hotkeys}**) that brings Flow forward from any app and puts it away again while it's in front. While it's **{assistant}**, that key is the hotkey's and no longer opens the assistant's panel. **Press a key…**, last among them, takes the next key you press instead: a letter, a digit, **`**, Space or an F key, held with ⌃, ⌥ or ⌘ on the Mac (Ctrl, Alt, or the Windows key or Super elsewhere), or an F key alone. The hotkey set is let go meanwhile, so it can be pressed too, and Esc keeps it.

With **Drop down** on, it drops the window over the top of the screen, in front, as a Quake console does (on the Mac on every Space, until the hotkey puts it away); off, Flow comes forward where it was. Either way, it stays in front of other windows only while **Always on top** (the title bar's **on-top**) is on. While it drops, **Drop-down height** says how much of the screen it takes, from a third to all of it; **Slide** has it slide down from above the screen and back up (at once in efficient mode, and on Wayland); **Put away when unfocused** puts it away once another app has the keys; and on the Mac, **Over full-screen apps** drops it over an app in full screen too, Flow's Dock icon and menu bar going while it's down. Where the key can't be taken, the line at the foot says why; on Linux it works on X11, not on Wayland.

# Notifications
**Notify when done**, under Terminal, has a command that ran at least that long (30 s at first) and finishes while Flow isn't in front tell you so: on the Mac a notification under the tab's name, whose click brings Flow forward with that tab in front; on Windows a notification the same way (where Windows has them off for Flow, its taskbar button flashes until you come back instead); on Linux a desktop notification. Flow plays no cue of its own for it then. Off sends none.

# Restart
**Restart**, at the end, starts Flow afresh without quitting it: every tab closes, ending what runs in them, config.toml is read again, and each tab opens again with its shell, its theme and its folder, greeting you as Flow does when it starts, with the startup logo and a theme's start screen. The window, the assistant's conversation and the [command history](help:history) stay. {restart} restarts only the tab in front. Under Terminal, **Reopen tabs at start** brings back the tabs open when Flow last quit, in the same way.

# From the shell
In a tab, `flow-settings` lists these settings by their names in config.toml, and gets, sets and resets them (`flow-settings --help`); Flow applies and saves each change, and says so. The assistant's settings, your own theme and the themes you saved are Settings' alone.

picker.title: Picking a color
picker.body: The square picks how strong and how light the color is, and the bar beside it its hue: click or drag in either. ←→ move the hue and ↑↓ the brightness (with Shift, further), or type a hex value such as `#41FF6E`. Enter or **Done** keeps the color, and Esc puts back the one before. Each color row in [Settings](help:settings) opens it.

gallery.title: The theme gallery
gallery.body:
The gallery shows the packages of themes in flowapp's catalog, and those you've installed, before you install them. Settings' **Theme gallery**, under Theme, opens it; Esc closes it.

# Looking
Choose a package on the left, and its themes come beside it: Flow fetches the package (a few kilobytes), checks it against the catalog and Flow's own key, and reads it as an install would, installing nothing. Choose a theme to see its look: its screen in its colors, the first lines of its start screen and its prompt, its sixteen colors, its font and whether it has a tube. The words are in Flow's own font until it's installed. ↑↓ choose in the list that has the keys, and ← and → (or Tab) move between the packages and the themes.

# Installing and wearing
**Install** installs the package, as `flowapp install` does in a tab ([Flow's apps](help:apps)), and its themes come into Settings' Theme row and the new-tab picker at once. Once it's installed, **Wear** wears the theme chosen, as the Theme row does, and **Upgrade** comes where a newer version is out. Enter does the first button. A package that needs a newer Flow says so, and waits for Flow to be updated.

key.title: The API key
key.body:
The assistant needs a key from the provider chosen in [Settings](help:settings): Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's GPT or Google's Gemini. Paste it ({dialog_paste}) and press Enter: it's checked with the provider by a free call, then kept in the system's store for passwords (the Keychain, Credential Manager or the Secret Service), never in a file. Esc closes this without one; Flow works as a terminal without any key.

Each provider keeps its own key, and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `GEMINI_API_KEY` in the environment takes its place. {key} changes the key later, and `/forget` in the [assistant's panel](help:assistant) removes it.

model.title: A 3D model from a file
model.body:
A program in one of the tabs asked Flow to show a file as a 3D model. That means reading a file the program chose, so Flow asks first, naming the tab and the file. **Allow** (Enter) reads it and shows the model; **Don't Allow** (Esc) doesn't. A relative path is from the shell's folder. Only a file on this computer is asked about: a path beginning with two slashes or backslashes (another computer's, `\\server\share\…`), and on Windows any path but a drive's (`C:\…`), isn't asked about or read, since on Windows opening a file on another computer would hand that computer your sign-in.

A model the program sends itself, rather than naming a file, doesn't ask.

about.title: About Flow
about.body:
The card shows Flow's version and its build, over a cube of its own rolling in 3D. Esc, Enter, Space or a click outside it closes it. **Release notes**, beside the version, opens its release's page on GitHub, with what's new in it; a Flow built from source opens the list of releases. **Resources**, beside **Release notes**, shows what each tab uses (its programs, their memory and CPU, its scrollback, its pictures and what they take on the GPU), Flow's own memory and CPU, what the window takes on the GPU and the frames drawn each second, read about once a second while it's open; resting the pointer on a tab, or bringing it to the front with the keys, shows the same for that tab in a card under it. Esc closes it.

**Restart Flow** closes every tab and opens each again, with its shell, its theme and its folder, as Flow does when it starts, after reading config.toml again, without quitting ([Settings](help:settings)' **Restart** does the same; {restart} restarts only the tab in front). **Legal** says whose the logos Flow shows are, on a [page of its own](help:legal). **Arcanii**, in the credits under the tagline, opens the GitHub page of Arcanii, who make Flow.

# Updates
- **On the Mac and Windows**, Flow's updater checks by itself and offers a new version when there is one; on the Mac, **Check for Updates…** in the Flow menu asks now.
- **On Linux**, a Flow installed by its `install.sh` updates itself from this card: its button checks, installs and restarts. A Flow from the .deb opens the release's page instead, and one from the AUR says a new version is out, for your AUR helper to install. Whether it checks once a day by itself is [asked once](help:updates), and changed later in Settings' **Update checks**.

Every update is signed with Flow's own key, and one that isn't is never installed.

updates.title: Checking for updates
updates.body:
Flow can look once a day for a newer release, reading its list of releases on GitHub, and say so in the title bar when there is one.

**Check Automatically** (Enter) looks once a day, when Flow starts and when it comes to the front; **Don't Check** (Esc) leaves it to you, in [About](help:about). Nothing is installed until you say so in About, and only an update signed with Flow's own key. [Settings](help:settings)' **Update checks** changes your answer later.

Once an update you started is in place (put there by Flow, or by apt in its own tab for the .deb) and About isn't open, a card asks whether to restart into it: **Restart Now** (Enter) closes this window and opens the new Flow with your tabs as they are, each in its folder, ending any program still running in one; **Later** (Esc) leaves it to About or the title bar's ↻.

shells.title: A new tab
shells.body:
The **+** after the tabs opens a tab at once with the default shell, in the theme Settings has, as {new_tab} does. The **…** beside it opens this picker, to choose both: the shells Flow found on this computer on the left, every theme on the right (Flow's, the old machines', your own and those you saved), the default shell and Settings' theme chosen to start with.
- ↑↓, or the wheel over a list, choose in it, and ←→ (or Tab) go between the two. A list longer than the window has room for shows what fits around its choice.
- Enter, or **Open tab**, opens a tab with the shell and the theme chosen; a click chooses, and a second click on what's chosen opens it.
- **Save as theme…** keeps what the window wears now, the tab in front's theme if it has one, under a name you type over [Settings](help:settings), to choose here and there.
- Anything else closes the picker, and the key does what it would have.

A tab in a theme of its own says so in its name, and the window wears that theme while the tab is in front: its colors, fonts, glass and CRT, its start screen and prompt, and its machine's sounds. Programs in it are told its colors when they ask. [Settings](help:settings) opens on the tab in front, and its look's sections change that tab alone; on **New tabs** they change the look the **+** opens with.

[Settings](help:settings)' **Default shell** picks which shell + opens. {pick_tab} shows tab 1 to 9, and {close_tab} closes the one in front (the last closes Flow).

tabs.title: The tab sidebar
tabs.body:
{sidebar} brings the tab sidebar out over the terminal, as do the three lines left of the tabs in the title bar, **Tab Sidebar** in the [command palette](help:palette) and, on the Mac, **View → Tab Sidebar**. It lists every tab in the title bar's order, each group's under its header, and under each tab what it's doing: a program's progress, the command running, how the last one ended (✓ or ✗), or, in a git checkout, the branch it's on, else its folder. The tab in front is lit, and a split tab folds open to show its panes.

# Choosing
Click a tab, or press Enter on it, and it comes to the front, the sidebar staying out so you can look at another; a pane's row brings that pane to the front in its tab. Esc, {sidebar} again or a click outside the sidebar puts it away. Resting the pointer on a tab's row shows what its programs use, as in the title bar.

# Keys
- ↑ and ↓ move through the rows, Page Up and Page Down by eight, Home and End to the ends; a letter goes to the next row whose name starts with it.
- Enter brings a tab or a pane forward, or folds a group open or shut.
- → and ← fold a group or a split tab open or shut; ← on a group's tab goes to its header.
- F2 names the row's tab or group, typed in its row: Enter keeps the name, Esc puts back the one before.
- {sidebar_move} moves the tab a step up or down, into the next group or out of its own at a group's edge, or a whole group past what's beside it.
- {sidebar_close} closes the row's tab, or its group; where something runs in it, it says what, and pressing it again closes it.
- Every other key of Flow's still works.

# Several tabs at once
{jump}-click a tab's row to pick it, with the row the keys were on, and again to let it go; Shift-click, or Shift with ↑ and ↓, picks every tab from where the pick began. A plain click or arrow, or Esc, lets them go. With tabs picked, **New Group** at the foot puts them all into one new group, gathered at the first one's place, and a picked row's **…** moves them all to a group, takes them out of theirs, or closes them.

# Dragging
Drag a tab's row to move it, a line showing where it will land. Dropped on a group's header, it goes into that group, after its tabs; between rows, it goes there, into the group where the line is set in and in the group's color, loose where it isn't, so the gap after a group's last tab takes it out of the group. Drag a group's header to move the whole group between other groups and loose tabs. A tab's pill in the title bar drags too: over a group's pills it joins that group, over a loose pill or a group's outer edge it lands loose, a line between the pills showing where; and a tab dragged from the bar can land in a pinned sidebar, or one from the sidebar in the bar. Esc, or letting go away from both, leaves it where it was.

# Pinned
The pin at the sidebar's foot (or **Tab sidebar** in [Settings](help:settings)) keeps it out beside the terminal, which narrows for it. The keys stay with the pane in front: {sidebar} moves them into the sidebar and back out, choosing a tab gives that tab the keys, and Esc or a click on the terminal gives them back. Drag its right edge to make it wider or narrower. The pin leans over while it isn't pinned and stands pressed in while it is; the pin again unpins it, leaving it out over the terminal until Esc or a click outside it puts it away. In a window too narrow to leave the terminal 20 columns, it pops out instead.

# Groups
A group's header has its color, its name and how many tabs it holds; click it to fold it shut or open. **New Group** at the sidebar's foot puts the tab in front into a group of its own, its name ready to be typed. A row's **…** opens its menu: for a tab, Rename, Move to another group or a new one, Remove from Group, Restart Tab and Close; for a group, Rename, its color, Theme…, Ungroup (its tabs stay where they are) and Close Group. **Theme…** lists the themes the new-tab picker does, with Settings' theme first: a group's tabs wear its theme unless one has a theme of its own (given it in the new-tab picker, or changed in Settings on that tab), a tab moved into the group puts it on and one moved out takes it off, and new tabs opened from the group start in it. A tab already open takes the theme's colors, font and screen at once, and its prompt and start screen with its next shell (Restart Tab). Close Group closes every tab in it at once while each waits at its prompt; where one is busy, or the group holds every tab so Flow would quit, it says so, and pressing it again closes them. A double click on a tab's or a group's name names it too.

Flow keeps the groups, their colors, their themes and which are folded with the tabs it opens again.

outside.title: Outside apps
outside.body:
Outside apps (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor) can use Flow through **flow-mcp**, the MCP server Flow carries, as far as you allow each one.

# Connecting
Turn on Settings' **Let outside apps connect**, under Outside apps. Off, Flow doesn't listen for them at all, and either way nothing listens on the network: flow-mcp reaches Flow through a socket (a pipe on Windows) only you can open. Each end asks the system who is at the other first: Flow closes a connection from another user unread, and flow-mcp sends nothing to anything but your own Flow, telling the app so. **Connect an app**, under it, gives flow-mcp's path, with **Copy for Claude Code** (the `claude mcp add` command to paste in a terminal) and **Copy JSON** (an `mcpServers` entry for Claude Desktop, Cursor and others). When an app calls and Flow isn't running, flow-mcp starts it.

# What an app may do
The first time an app calls, a card asks what it may do: read your tabs and panes (and Flow's help), open, close and bring forward tabs and panes, change Flow's settings, and run commands. Switch each with a click or 1 to 4; Enter allows, and Esc denies, so it may do nothing and isn't asked again. Flow knows each app by its name and the program that started flow-mcp: another program giving the same name is asked about anew. Settings' Outside apps lists each one, a switch for each thing it may do, and **Forget**, to be asked again.

This keeps apps from doing what you didn't mean them to. A program already running as you could do anything anyway.

# Commands
An app runs commands only in panes of its own: one Flow opens beside yours, labeled with its name, or the tabs and panes it opened. It may read your panes, but it never types into your shells nor closes your tabs. **Run commands** is **Off**, **Ask each time** (a card shows the command: Enter runs it, Esc skips it) or **Without asking**. A command Flow's rules rate high risk (deleting, sudo, erasing a disk, turning off the system's protections, sending data to another machine, naming a file that looks like a secret) always asks, whatever the app may do. The rules go by pattern, not a sandbox, so **Without asking** runs what they don't recognize.

# Settings
An app allowed to change settings changes what `flow-settings` may ([Settings](help:settings)): the look, in the tab in front, and the sound and the window, for every tab. The assistant's settings and your themes stay closed to it.

apps.title: Flow's apps
apps.body:
`flowapp`, in any tab, installs Flow's apps and keeps them up to date as Homebrew keeps its formulae: Flow Rogue, Flow Mines, Flow Invaders, and `flow-sdk`, the SDK for C and Python with its demos. Flow itself carries none of them, so `flowapp install flow-rogue` is how a game comes.

# Keeping up to date
- `flowapp update` reads the catalog of apps and says which have a newer version.
- `flowapp upgrade` installs those, or only the ones named (`flowapp upgrade flow-rogue`).
- `flowapp outdated` says again what's newer, from the catalog last read.

`upgrade` and `install` read the catalog again before they download, since one read before a release can name a download that's gone; offline, they go by the one last read and say so. `list`, `outdated`, `info` and `search` go by the one last read: `info` says when that was, and the others say so once it's a day old.

An app's download can need a newer Flow than yours, as the catalog says: `install` refuses it and `upgrade` leaves it until Flow is updated, saying which Flow it needs, and `outdated` and `info` say so too.

What flowapp installs goes in a folder of your own, `apps/` beside config.toml, which every tab's PATH has, so a tab already open runs it too. Flow carried Flow Rogue and Flow Mines itself until 0.1.33, and an update from such a Flow keeps them: its first start installs them with flowapp (or the next, if it was offline). A copy an older Flow left counts as installed, at its own version, and upgrading it puts the newer one ahead of it.

# Installing and removing
- `flowapp install <app>` installs one (`flowapp install flow-sdk`), and says where the SDK's library, C header and Python package are.
- `flowapp remove <app>` takes off one flowapp installed; your saves and settings stay.
- `flowapp list` says what you have and its versions, `flowapp info <app>` what an app is, and `flowapp search` (with words, or none) the apps there are.

In a terminal these are tables, a newer version in green, and a download shows how far it's got on one line, with a ✓ once it's checked. Piped, they're plain lines that a script can read, and with `--json` (`flowapp list --json`) they're JSON.

# Ahead of the system's commands
What flowapp installs comes after the system's commands on the PATH, so an app's `ls` never takes the place of the system's unasked. `flowapp first <app>` puts an app's programs (or one, by its name, or `<app>/<program>` where two apps have one of that name) ahead of them in Flow's tabs, and `flowapp last <app>` (or `--all`) puts the system's first again. The tab you ran it in goes by it at its next prompt, and another tab open now once its prompt comes back.

Each can say where and how:
- `--shell zsh,bash` puts it first in those shells alone, `--except powershell` in all but that one. The shells are `zsh`, `bash` (every bash, Git Bash's too), `sh`, `powershell`, `cmd` and `busybox`. A later choice takes an earlier one's place in the shells it names, and leaves the rest.
- `--here` puts it first (or, with `last`, takes it out) in this tab alone, until the tab closes.
- `--prompt` puts it first at the prompt alone, as an alias, so scripts run from a tab keep the system's command; without it, it's first on the PATH, which scripts find too. cmd has no hook at its prompt, so it isn't first there.
- `--take` says what of the shell's own it takes away while it's first, and gives back after: `builtin` (bash's and zsh's `echo`, `printf`, `pwd`; not `cd` or `export`, which no program can do the work of), `alias` (PowerShell's own, and those your startup files make in bash, zsh and BusyBox, such as `ls --color=auto`), `function` (PowerShell's `mkdir`), `applet` (BusyBox's), or `none`. By default it takes PowerShell's alias and BusyBox's applet, nothing else. cmd's own commands (`dir`, `type`) nothing puts aside.

`flowapp first` alone lists, for each shell, each name first there, how, what it took away, and what of the shell's own still comes ahead of it (`--json` for scripts). Your own aliases and functions it can't see: `type <name>` in a tab says what runs there (`Get-Command <name> -All` in PowerShell). A BusyBox tab follows a change once `flowapp` runs in it.

# Themes
A package of themes installs as an app does (`flowapp install flow-core-themes`, Flow's own machines, kept up to date), and its themes come in Settings' Theme row and the new-tab picker once Flow is in front again; one with a built-in machine's name takes that one's place. `flowapp install mine.tar.gz` installs a package of your own from its file. A theme is only colors, fonts, pictures and words to type, never a program, so one of your own needs no signature, and one holding a program is refused.

# Skills
A package of skills installs as one of themes does (`flowapp install flow-skills`, Flow's own skills for its [assistant](help:assistant)), and an app may carry skills beside its programs. They're listed in Settings' Skills section, each off until you turn it on there, so installing an app never changes what the assistant reads; the install says so. `flowapp install mine.tar.gz` installs a package of your own: a `skills.json` naming it and its version, and a `skills/` folder of skills.

# In Settings
Settings' Apps lists them too: each app and package of themes or skills you have or the catalog offers, with Install, Upgrade and Remove (pressed twice) that do what flowapp would. Catalog says when the catalog was read, and Check now reads it again. Check apps at start and Check apps (daily or weekly) have Flow read it by itself and say when an app you have has a newer version; it never upgrades one by itself. The first start of a newer Flow reminds you to check them.

The app chosen ends its hint saying who signed it, as `flowapp info` does, and a row adds **not signed** for a package of your own, or **unknown key** for a key Flow doesn't know; one Flow signed stays as it is. An app that introduces itself (below) does so in a tab of its own once Settings has installed it.

# Safety
The catalog is in Flow's public releases, beside its own updates, and before anything is put in place each download's size and checksum are checked against the catalog's, and its signature against Flow's own key; one that doesn't match is never unpacked.

`flowapp list` and `search` say who signed each download, the first digits of the key's fingerprint and when it was signed, as the catalog says: Flow's key, `f186 6b49`. `flowapp info <app>` gives the whole fingerprint, when flowapp checked the download, and on the Mac who signed its programs, as `codesign` says; then the lines that check the signature with OpenSSL 3 or later alone, trusting nothing of flowapp's. `flowapp verify` (or `flowapp verify <app>`) fetches what you have again, checks it, and looks at every file installed against it: a file changed or gone is said, and so is one added since, which doesn't count.

# flowapp itself
flowapp is in the catalog too, with a version of its own (`flowapp --version`), so a newer one comes out without a new Flow. `flowapp outdated` offers it and `flowapp upgrade` installs it like any app; from then on it runs in Flow's tabs in place of the one your Flow carries, and `flowapp remove flowapp` goes back to that one. Whichever is newer runs, so a later Flow that carries a newer flowapp runs its own. A tab opened before the upgrade may still run the old one: open a new tab, or in bash or zsh type `hash -r`.

# An app introducing itself
An app's download can hold a `flowapp.json` naming one of its own programs to run once it's installed, so what runs is covered by Flow's signature, never by the catalog. `flowapp install` runs it after a fresh install alone, in a terminal alone (never from a script, a pipe or the assistant), and not for an upgrade; `flowapp hello <app>` runs it again. flow-say asks whether to fetch its voice, a download of its own, asking how to address you meanwhile, then greets you aloud as Flow, by your name and the time of day ("Good afternoon, Alex. I am Flow.") or in another of its greetings.

command.title: The flow command
command.body:
`flow`, in one of Flow's tabs, opens a new tab in the Flow that tab belongs to and types a command there: `flow ssh -N -L 7445:127.0.0.1:7445 me@host` keeps a tunnel open in a tab of its own while you go on in this one.

The new tab is like the one you typed it in: the same shell, the same theme, and the folder `flow` ran in. It opens right after that tab and comes to the front, and the command is typed once its shell waits at its prompt, as if you'd typed it there: it goes into the command history, and the shell stays when it ends. `flow` alone opens a tab at its prompt.

# Options
- `--split` opens a pane beside the one you typed it in, in its tab, rather than a tab.
- `--behind` opens it without coming to the front, so the keys stay where they are.
- `--close` closes it once the command ends well. A failure leaves it open, so its error can be read, and so does stopping it with Ctrl+C. cmd can't say how a command ended, so there it closes whenever the command ends.
- `--shell <name>` and `--theme <name>` pick another shell or theme, by its id or its name (`flow --shell bash --theme green htop`).
- `--window` starts a Flow of its own for the command (below).

The first word that isn't an option begins the command, and `--` ends the options, for a command that begins with `-`.

# Words and quotes
Each word goes to the new shell as the shell you typed it in gave it to `flow`, after it expanded its own variables, globs and quotes. A plain word goes as it is; any other is quoted, so the new shell expands nothing in it again, not even cmd's `%NAME%`. A word holding a control character (a tab, a line break, Esc, Ctrl+C and the like) is refused, since typed at a prompt it would be a key, not a letter: put a command that needs one in a script. Letters past ASCII go as letters: Flow's bash hook has bash's line editor take them as letters, not keys, in a locale that isn't UTF-8 too. Where the new shell hasn't shown Flow's prompt when the command is typed, or bash's hook says its prompt may take them as keys (its locale has just changed) or can't run before its prompts (a read-only `PROMPT_COMMAND`), they go into zsh and bash as their bytes (`$'\xc3\xbc'` for ü). A word holding a `~` is quoted, since bash expands one after a `=` (`--prefix=~/x`).

# A Flow of its own
`flow --window <command>`, or `flow` run outside Flow's tabs (another terminal, a script, a shortcut), starts a new Flow with that one tab, a guest beside the Flow you have. It opens none of your saved tabs and saves none, takes no hotkey, doesn't listen for outside apps and doesn't check for updates, all of which stay the first Flow's. It quits when its last tab closes.

# Only from Flow's own tabs
Anything that prints in a tab could print the question `flow` asks, a file you `cat` or a remote host over ssh among them. So each pane has a secret of its own, which only programs started in it have, and Flow opens a tab only for a question that carries the asking pane's secret. Any other it doesn't answer at all, not even to say no, since its answer would be typed at the prompt. So where nothing answers, `flow` says the secret it sent may be another pane's; through tmux or screen, which don't pass Flow's questions on, nothing answers either.

Another program called `flow` that comes earlier on the PATH (the JavaScript type checker's, say) runs instead of Flow's.

server_ask.title: A server asks
server_ask.body:
An MCP server the assistant uses (see [the assistant](help:assistant)) may ask you something while it works, and the card in front names it. Flow sends what you answer to that server alone, never to the assistant's model itself, though the server may put it in what its tool hands back.

# A form
Its fields come in the server's order, those it needs marked *. Tab and Shift+Tab, or ↑ and ↓, go from field to field and on to the buttons. Type in a field of text or numbers; Space turns a switch over and picks the option you're on; ← and → move along a field's options. Enter goes on to the next field, and on the last one sends, as Ctrl+Enter or ⌘Enter does from anywhere. **Send** checks each field first, as the server asked (its length, its form, a number's range), and says under a field what's wrong. **Decline** says no; Esc puts the card away without an answer.

A prompt run from the panel (`/<server>:<prompt>`) asks this way for what it needs that you didn't type after its name.

# A link
A server may ask you to open a page (to sign in to something of its own, say). The card shows the whole address, its host lit, and warns where the host may pass for another or the page isn't HTTPS. **Open in Browser** opens it in your own browser; Flow never opens it unless you say, and never reads it. **Decline** says no.

Where a call can't go on until you've been there, its card in the panel waits for you, with **Try Again** and **Give Up**; Flow makes the call again once the server says you're done.

flowapp.usage:
Flow's apps, kept up to date from the shell: its games, its SDK, its themes and skills for its assistant.

  flowapp update            reads the catalog of apps, and says what's newer
  flowapp upgrade [app…]    installs what's newer of what you have
  flowapp install <app…>    installs an app or a package of themes or skills
  flowapp install <file.tar.gz>  installs a package of themes or skills of your own
  flowapp remove <app…>     takes off an app flowapp installed
  flowapp list              what you have, and its versions
  flowapp outdated          what has a newer version
  flowapp info <app>        what an app is
  flowapp search [word…]    the apps there are
  flowapp verify [app…]     fetches what you have again and checks it's as downloaded
  flowapp hello <app>       has an app introduce itself again, where it can (flow-say says hello aloud)
  flowapp first [app…]      puts an app's programs ahead of the system's commands of their names, in Flow's tabs (alone: says what's first in each shell, and what still comes ahead)
  flowapp last <app…>       puts the system's first again (--all for every one)

first and last take a program by its name too, or <app>/<program> where two apps have one of that name, and:
  --shell <shell,…>         in these shells alone (zsh, bash, sh, powershell, cmd, busybox)
  --except <shell,…>        in every shell but these
  --here                    in this tab alone, until it closes
  --prompt                  (first) at the prompt alone, so scripts keep the system's command
  --take <what,…>           (first) what of the shell's own it takes away: alias, builtin, function, applet, or none (by default PowerShell's alias and BusyBox's applet)

With --json, update, list, outdated, info, search and first print what they list as JSON, for scripts.

Flow carries none of them: install the ones you want (an update from a Flow that carried Flow Rogue and Flow Mines installs those). Every download is checked against the catalog and Flow's own signature before it's put in place. list and search say who signed each, with which key and when, info how to check that yourself with OpenSSL, and verify whether what's installed is still as downloaded. An app new here may introduce itself once it's installed in a tab, as its download says (flow-say asks first, since its voice is a download of its own). Themes come in Settings' Theme row and the new-tab picker once Flow is in front again; a package of your own isn't signed, but a theme is only colors, fonts and words, never a program. A package's skills for the assistant stay off until Settings' Skills section turns them on.

flow_mcp.usage:
Flow as an MCP server, so an outside app (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor) can use Flow as far as you allow.

An app's MCP config runs flow-mcp; it isn't run by hand. Turn on Settings → Outside apps in Flow, then add it to the app:

  Claude Code:     claude mcp add flow -- <the path below>
  Claude Desktop:  an entry named flow under mcpServers, its command the path below

The first time the app calls, Flow asks you what it may do: read your tabs, open and close tabs, change Flow's settings, run commands in panes of its own. Settings → Outside apps changes or forgets that later. Where Flow isn't running, flow-mcp starts it.

flow_settings.usage:
Flow's settings, seen and changed from the shell, in one of Flow's tabs.

  flow-settings                    every setting a program may see, with its value
  flow-settings get <key>          one of them, such as fx.style
  flow-settings set <key> <value>  changes one: rain, 16, true, "#00ff00", '["VT323", "Menlo"]'
  flow-settings reset <key>        puts one back to its default (reset all: every one)
  flow-settings reset terminal     starts this tab afresh: its screen, scrollback and modes
  flow-settings restart            restarts Flow, as Settings' Restart does, while no other tab or pane runs a program

Flow answers only programs run in its own tabs, which carry the tab's key (FLOW_TAB_KEY), and anything else not at all. Flow saves each change and says so. The look's settings, the theme among them, are this tab's, as Settings opened on it has them; the rest are Flow's, for every tab. The assistant's settings, your own theme and the themes you saved are Settings' alone.
flow_settings.takes: What each setting takes, as Flow says (where Settings offers choices or a range):
flow_settings.no_key: flow-settings: this shell has no tab key (FLOW_TAB_KEY), so it asked nothing: Flow answers only programs run in its own tabs, which have one. sudo and env -i leave it out, and ssh doesn't carry it.
flow_settings.no_answer: flow-settings: Flow didn't answer. tmux and screen don't pass Flow's questions on, so from inside one nothing reaches it. Or the key here (FLOW_TAB_KEY) is another's, since Flow answers only what carries this pane's own: another pane's, or one an ssh session or a script brought along. Or this terminal isn't one of Flow's tabs, though it was started from one.
flow_settings.reset_all: Every setting a program may change is back to its default.

flow_command.usage:
Opens a tab in the Flow this tab belongs to, like this one (its shell, its theme, this folder), and types a command there once its shell waits at its prompt.

  flow [options] [--] <command> [args…]   a new tab that runs the command
  flow [options]                          a new tab here, at its prompt
  flow --window [options] <command>       a Flow of its own for it

  --split          a pane beside this one, rather than a tab
  --behind         opens without coming to the front
  --close          closes once the command ends well (a failure leaves it open to read)
  --shell <name>   another shell, by its id or its name (zsh, bash, powershell, cmd…)
  --theme <name>   another theme, by its id or its name
  --window         a new Flow with that one tab, beside the one running

The first word that isn't an option begins the command, and -- ends the options. Each word goes to the new shell as this shell gave it to flow, quoted so it isn't expanded again. A word holding a control character (a tab, a line break, Esc) is refused: typed, it would be a key. flow returns once the tab is open, before its command runs. Outside Flow's tabs (another terminal, a script, a shortcut) it starts a Flow of its own, as --window does: one that keeps no saved tabs, hotkey, outside apps or updates of its own.
